title: Why does sunlight make you sneeze? Aristotle got it wrong
description:
About one in four people sneeze when they step into bright sunlight. Aristotle blamed the sun's heat on the nose; in the 1600s Francis Bacon faced the sun with his eyes shut, didn't sneeze, and showed it was the light, then blamed 'the moisture of the brain'. A 2010 EEG study found sneezers' visual cortex reacts more strongly to light, and a 2025 review says the mechanism is still unclear.

Sources:
- Photic sneeze reflex — Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photic_sneeze_reflex
- Aristotle: Problems with the Nose (from Barnes, The Complete Works of Aristotle, Princeton 1984) — Memorial University of Newfoundland: https://mun.ca/biology/scarr/Aristotle_on_Sneezing.html
- Sneezing At The Sun (A Moment of Science) — Indiana Public Media / Indiana University: https://indianapublicmedia.org/amomentofscience/sneezing-at-the-sun/
- When the Sun Prickles Your Nose: An EEG Study Identifying Neural Bases of Photic Sneezing (Langer, Beeli & Jäncke, 2010) — PLoS ONE: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0009208
- Stimulus conditions eliciting sneezing in response to bright light (Exp Brain Res 2025): Europe PMC record — Europe PMC (EMBL-EBI): https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:39893297%20AND%20SRC:MED&resultType=core&format=json

'About one in four' is an estimate; studies range from about 18% to 35%. Aristotle and Bacon are named, not depicted. The characters are cartoons, not medical advice.
